API Reference Portfolio This portal is a working mockup of a developer-facing API reference. It shows how I design, build, and maintain documentation that a third-party developer can integrate against without a support ticket. The content mirrors the API documentation I wrote and maintained in a fintech environment with Swagger/OpenAPI. The examples cover the usual business domains: reference data (Accounts, Portfolios) and asset management (Transactions, Payments). All examples use the demonstration base URL https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1. The API is not live. Getting Started 🔐 Authentication OAuth 2.0 Bearer tokens for the production and UAT environments. 📐 Conventions Pagination, filtering, rate limits, idempotency, versioning, and data formats. ⚠️ Errors Error envelope, the full status code catalogue, and safe retry patterns. 📄 OpenAPI Specification The machine-readable contract, and the reference generated from it. Reference Data 👤 Accounts Create, read, update, and delete Custodian Accounts. 📊 Portfolios Manage Portfolios across all Custodians. 🏛️ Custodians Banks, prime brokers, and clearing houses that hold your assets. Financial Operations 💳 Transactions Submit and process Transactions: wires, money market, securities, FX, cashflows, loan tranches. 🏦 Payments Initiate and settle Payments over SWIFT, SEPA, Faster Payments, and internal rails. Reference Data Accounts Create and manage Accounts in your environment. The API supports full CRUD operations. For Account management, Account parameters, and reference data in the DZ environment, see the Reference Data User Guide. Pagination, filtering, and idempotency work the same way here as everywhere else: see Conventions and Errors. GET/accounts List accounts Returns a paginated list of Accounts. Filter by status to narrow results. Query parameters Parameter Type Required Description limit integer Optional Results per page. Default: 20. Maximum: 100. offset integer Optional Results to skip before the page starts. Default: 0. status string Optional Filter by Account status. One of: active, suspended, closed. cURLPythonJavaScript RequestCopy curl -X GET "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts?limit=20&offset=0&status=active" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" Response fields Field Type Description data array The page of Account objects. Empty when nothing matches, never null. total integer Total Accounts matching the filter, across all pages. limit integer The limit applied to this response, after clamping to 100. offset integer The offset applied to this response. Response200 OK { "data": [ { "id": "acc_007", "owner_id": "james_b", "name": "BHMS Account 007", "type": "fee", "currency": "GBP", "balance": 12500000, "status": "active", "created_at": "2026-03-15T10:30:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-03-20T14:22:00Z" }, { "id": "acc_006", "owner_id": "alec_t", "name": "Operating Account", "type": "operating", "currency": "GBP", "balance": 42000000, "status": "active", "created_at": "2026-03-15T10:30:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-03-20T14:22:00Z" } ], "total": 2, "limit": 20, "offset": 0 } GET/accounts/{id} Get account by ID Retrieves the full details of a single Account by its unique identifier. Path parameters Parameter Type Required Description id string Required The unique Account ID, for example acc_007. cURLPythonJavaScript RequestCopy curl -X GET "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts/acc_007" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" Response fields — Account object Field Type Description id string Unique Account identifier. Opaque, do not parse it. owner_id string Identifier of the user who owns this Account. name string Human-readable label shown in the UI. type string Purpose the Account serves. One of: trading, operating, custody, fee. Fixed at creation. currency string ISO 4217 code. Fixed at creation. balance number Current balance in the major unit of currency. status string One of: active, suspended, closed. created_at string RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC. updated_at string RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC of the last change. Response200 OK { "id": "acc_007", "owner_id": "james_b", "name": "BHMS Account 007", "type": "fee", "currency": "GBP", "balance": 12500000, "status": "active", "created_at": "2026-03-15T10:30:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-03-20T14:22:00Z" } POST/accounts Create account Creates an Account for the specified owner and returns the created resource. Request body Parameter Type Required Description owner_id string Required ID of the user who owns this Account. name string Required Human-readable label for the Account. type string Required Account type. One of: trading, operating, custody, fee. Cannot be changed later. currency string Required ISO 4217 currency code, for example USD, EUR, GBP. Cannot be changed later. Send an Idempotency-Key header so a retry after a timeout returns the original Account instead of creating a second one. cURLPythonJavaScript RequestCopy curl -X POST "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: 5f2b8c14-9d7a-4e31-b6c0-1a2f3e4d5c6b" \ -d '{ "owner_id": "james_b", "name": "Main Trading Account", "type": "trading", "currency": "USD" }' Response fields — Account object Field Type Description id string Unique Account identifier. Opaque, do not parse it. owner_id string Identifier of the user who owns this Account. name string Human-readable label shown in the UI. type string Purpose the Account serves. One of: trading, operating, custody, fee. Fixed at creation. currency string ISO 4217 code. Fixed at creation. balance number Current balance in the major unit of currency. status string One of: active, suspended, closed. created_at string RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC. updated_at string RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC of the last change. Response201 Created { "id": "acc_007", "owner_id": "james_b", "name": "BHMS Account 007", "type": "fee", "currency": "GBP", "balance": 12500000, "status": "active", "created_at": "2026-03-15T10:30:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-03-20T14:22:00Z" } PATCH/accounts/{id} Update account Partially updates an Account. Only the fields you send are modified. Path parameters Parameter Type Required Description id string Required The unique Account ID. Request body Parameter Type Required Description name string Optional New display name for the Account. status string Optional New status. One of: active, suspended, closed. type and currency are fixed at creation. Sending either returns 422 validation_failed. cURLPythonJavaScript RequestCopy curl -X PATCH "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts/acc_007" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name": "Primary Custodian Account", "status": "active"}' Response fields — Account object Field Type Description id string Unique Account identifier. One of: trading, operating, custody, fee. Fixed at creation. currency string ISO 4217 code. Fixed at creation. balance number Current balance in the major unit of currency. status string One of: active, suspended, closed. created_at string RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC. updated_at string RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC of the last change. Response200 OK { "id": "acc_007", "owner_id": "james_b", "name": "Primary Custodian Account", "type": "fee", "currency": "GBP", "balance": 12500000, "status": "active", "created_at": "2026-03-15T10:30:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-04-01T09:00:00Z" } DELETE/accounts/{id} Remove account Permanently deletes an Account and all its associated data. This action cannot be undone. Path parameters Parameter Type Required Description id string Required The unique Account ID to delete. An Account that still holds an open Position returns 409 conflict. Close the Position first, then retry. cURLPythonJavaScript RequestCopy curl -X DELETE "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts/acc_007" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" Response204 No Content // No body returned

Legal & Compliance Credit Agreements Create and manage Credit Agreements linked to your Accounts. Each Agreement captures the legal and financial terms of a credit facility established between your organisation and a counterparty. Credit Agreements are scoped to an Account and are independent of Portfolios. A single Account may have multiple Credit Agreements with different counterparties, currencies, and maturity profiles. GET/agreements List credit agreements Returns a paginated list of Credit Agreements. Filter by account, status, or type to narrow results. Query parameters Parameter Type Required Description limit integer Optional Number of results to return. Default: 20, max: 100. offset integer Optional Number of results to skip. Use for pagination. Default: 0. account_id string Optional Filter agreements by the associated account ID. status string Optional Filter by status. One of: pending, active, terminated. type string Optional Filter by agreement type. Currently only: credit. cURLPythonJavaScript RequestCopy curl -X GET "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/agreements?limit=20&offset=0&status=active" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" Response fields Field Type Description data array The page of Credit Agreement objects. Empty when nothing matches, never null. total integer Total Agreements matching the filter, across all pages. limit integer The limit applied to this response, after clamping to 100. offset integer The offset applied to this response. Opaque, do not parse it. account_id string Account this Agreement is scoped to. Fixed at creation. type string Agreement type. One of: credit. Fixed at creation. name string Descriptive name shown in the UI and on statements. principal_amount number Facility principal in the major unit of currency. currency string ISO 4217 code. Getting Started Base URL & Authentication The API uses the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow. Every request must carry a short-lived Bearer token issued by the auth server. Tokens expire after 3600 seconds; when one expires, request a new token with the same client credentials. Base URLs Use the production URL for live integrations and the UAT URL for development and testing. Both environments expose the same API surface and use the same authentication flow. Environment Base URL Status Production https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1 Live UAT https://api.uat.dzenterprise.io/v1 Sandbox Authentication with OAuth 2.0 The API uses the client credentials grant type: your application authenticates with its own client_id and client_secret, with no user context. Tokens expire after 3600 seconds (1 hour). Cache the token and refresh it before it expires. Your App ──── POST /oauth/token ──────► Auth Server ◄── access_token ───────────── auth.api.dzenterprise.io. Your App ──── GET /accounts ─────────► API Server Authorization: Bearer … api.dzenterprise.io Step 1 — Obtain a token cURLPythonJavaScript POST /oauth/tokenCopy curl -X POST "https://auth.dzenterprise.io/oauth/token" \ -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \ -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \ -d "client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID" \ -d "client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET" \ -d "scope=api:read api:write" Response200 OK { "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600, "scope": "api:read api:write" } Step 2 — Authenticate requests Pass the token in the Authorization header on every request. The X-Request-ID header is optional but recommended: it correlates your logs with ours when you need to debug a call. cURLPythonJavaScript Authenticated requestCopy curl -X GET "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Request-ID: req_abc123" Required headers Header Value Notes Authorization Bearer {access_token} Required on every endpoint Content-Type application/json Required for POST / PATCH X-Request-ID Unique string Optional. Correlates logs for debugging Authentication errors A missing, malformed, or expired token returns 401 unauthorized. A valid token without the required scope returns 403 insufficient_scope. Both follow the shared error envelope described in Errors. Response401 Unauthorized { "error": "unauthorized", "message": "Bearer token is missing or has expired.", "status": 401, "request_id": "req_abc123" }

Getting Started Conventions Rules that hold across every endpoint: how collections are paged, filtered, and sorted; how rate limits and retries behave; how to make writes safe to repeat; and how the API versions and deprecates itself. Read this once and the endpoint pages become reference material rather than instructions. Pagination Every collection endpoint returns the same envelope and accepts the same two parameters. A limit above 100 is clamped to 100 rather than rejected, so always read the limit the response reports back rather than the one you sent. Pagination parameters Parameter Type Required Description limit integer Optional Results per page. Default: 20. Maximum: 100. offset integer Optional Results to skip before the page starts. Default: 0. List envelope Field Type Description data array The page of results. Empty when nothing matches the filter; never null. total integer Total number of records matching the filter, across all pages. limit integer The limit applied to this response, after clamping to the maximum. offset integer The offset applied to this response. Response200 OK { "data": [ "…" ], "total": 137, "limit": 20, "offset": 0 } Walking every page Stop when offset reaches total. Do not stop on a short page: a filter applied after paging can legitimately return fewer rows than the limit while more pages remain. cURLPythonJavaScript PaginationCopy curl -X GET "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts?limit=50&offset=100&sort=-created_at" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" Filtering and sorting Each endpoint documents its own filters, such as status on Accounts or account_id on Transactions. Multiple filters combine with AND. The parameters below work on every collection. Common query parameters Parameter Type Required Description sort string Optional Field to sort by. Prefix with a hyphen for descending order, for example -created_at. created_after string Optional RFC 3339 timestamp. Returns records created strictly after this instant. created_before string Optional RFC 3339 timestamp. Returns records created strictly before this instant. Results are sorted by -created_at unless you say otherwise, so the newest record comes first. Sorting is applied before paging. Rate limits Requests are limited per client, per environment: 600 requests per minute on production and 120 requests per minute on UAT. Exceeding the limit returns 429 rate_limit_exceeded. Every response carries your current budget, so you can throttle before you are throttled. Rate limit headers Field Type Description X-RateLimit-Limit integer Requests permitted in the current window. X-RateLimit-Remaining integer Requests still available in the current window. X-RateLimit-Reset integer Unix timestamp at which the window resets. Retry-After integer Sent with 429 only. Seconds to wait before retrying. See Errors for the retry pattern that honours Retry-After. Idempotency GET, PATCH, and DELETE are idempotent by definition: repeating them leaves the resource in the same state. POST is not, and a timeout leaves you unable to tell whether the resource was created. Send an Idempotency-Key header with every POST. Generate a UUID per logical operation, not per HTTP attempt, and reuse it on retries. The first request with a given key is processed; any later request with the same key returns the original response instead of creating a second resource. Keys are retained for 24 hours. cURLPythonJavaScript POST /transactionsCopy curl -X POST "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/transactions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: 5f2b8c14-9d7a-4e31-b6c0-1a2f3e4d5c6b" \ -d '{ "account_id": "acc_007", "type": "wire", "amount": 5000.00, "currency": "USD" }' Versioning and deprecation The major version is part of the path: /v1. It changes only for a breaking change, and two major versions run in parallel for at least twelve months. The following are not breaking changes, and your client must tolerate them without a release: A new field added to a response object. A new optional request parameter. A new value added to an existing enumeration. A new endpoint or a new error code. When an endpoint is deprecated, its responses carry a Deprecation header with the date it was announced and a Sunset header with the date it stops responding. Both are announced in the changelog before the header appears. Data formats The API accepts and returns application/json only, and field names are lower case with underscores. Formats used across the API Field Type Description Timestamps string RFC 3339 in UTC, for example 2026-03-15T10:30:00Z. Fields ending in _at are timestamps. Dates string ISO 8601 calendar dates without a time component, for example 2026-01-15. Fields ending in _date are dates. Money number Decimal in the major unit of the currency, for example 12500000.00 for GBP. Always paired with a currency field. Currency string ISO 4217 three-letter code in upper case, for example GBP. Identifiers string Opaque, prefixed strings such as acc_007 or prt_BNPParibas_001. Getting Started Errors Every failed request returns a standard HTTP status code and a JSON body with the same shape. Handle errors by switching on the error field, which is stable across releases, rather than on the message text, which is not. The error object All errors share one envelope. A 422 adds a details array naming each field that failed validation; every other error omits it. Error object Field Type Description error string Stable, machine-readable error code. Switch on this value, never on the message. message string Human-readable explanation. Wording may change between releases, so do not parse it. status integer HTTP status code, repeated in the body for clients that log bodies only. request_id string Identifier for this call. Quote it in any support request. details array Present on 422 only. One entry per rejected field, each with field and issue. Response422 Unprocessable Entity { "error": "validation_failed", "message": "The request contains one or more invalid fields.", "status": 422, "request_id": "req_9f3c21a7", "details": [ { "field": "currency", "issue": "Must be a valid ISO 4217 code." }, { "field": "maturity_date", "issue": "Must be later than start_date." } ] } Error codes The codes below apply to every endpoint. Endpoint pages list only the errors specific to that resource. Status codes and how to resolve them Status Error code What it means How to fix it 400 invalid_request The request could not be parsed: malformed JSON, an unknown query parameter, or a missing required field. Validate the request body against the schema and check that Content-Type is application/json. 401 unauthorized The Bearer token is missing, malformed, or has expired. Request a new token from the auth server and retry. Tokens expire after 3600 seconds. 403 insufficient_scope The token is valid but does not carry the scope this endpoint requires. Request a token with the required scope (for example api:write for POST, PATCH, and DELETE). 404 not_found No resource exists with the supplied identifier, or it is outside your environment. Check the identifier and confirm you are calling the environment the resource belongs to. 409 conflict The request conflicts with the current state of the resource, for example deleting an Account that still holds an open Position. Fetch the resource, resolve the conflicting state, then retry. 422 validation_failed The request was well formed but a field value is not acceptable, for example an unknown currency code or a maturity date in the past. Read the details array: it names every field that failed and why. 429 rate_limit_exceeded You have sent more requests than your plan allows in the current window. Back off and retry after the number of seconds given in the Retry-After header. 500 internal_error An unexpected error occurred on our side. The request was not processed. Retry with exponential backoff. If it persists, contact support with the request_id. 503 service_unavailable The service is temporarily unavailable, usually during a scheduled maintenance window. Retry after the interval given in the Retry-After header. Retrying safely Retry 429 and 5xx only. The remaining 4xx errors describe a problem with the request itself and will fail again on every attempt. When a response carries a Retry-After header, wait at least that many seconds; otherwise back off exponentially. Retry with backoff cURLPythonJavaScript Retry handlingCopy curl -i -X GET "https://api.dzenterprise.io/v1/accounts/acc_007" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer {access_token}" # HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests # Retry-After: 30 Reporting a problem Every response, successful or not, carries a request_id. Include it when you contact support: it resolves to the exact call in our logs and turns a diagnostic conversation into a lookup.

Financial Operations Payments Initiate and track Payments across four settlement rails: swift, sepa, faster_payments, and internal. The API supports full CRUD operations. A Payment debits an Account and settles through the Custodian that holds it. Where a Transaction records the intent to move value, a Payment is the instruction that actually moves the cash. One of: swift, sepa, faster_payments, internal. status string Optional Payment status. One of: pending, processing, settled, failed, returned, cancelled. currency string Optional Filter by ISO 4217 currency code. limit integer Optional Results per page. Default: 20. Maximum: 100. offset integer Optional Results to skip before the page starts. REST API for the DZ Enterprise treasury platform. This specification is a portfolio artifact: it describes a fictional API and no live server implements it. It exists to show how I model an API contract in OpenAPI and generate reference documentation from it. The hand-written reference at /api and this specification describe the same surface. Read the hand-written pages for narrative and worked examples, and this file for the machine-readable contract.

All requests and responses use application/json. Collections are paged with limit and offset and return a data/total envelope. Timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC. Dates are ISO 8601 without a time component. Monetary amounts are decimals in the major unit, always paired with a currency code. Every POST accepts an Idempotency-Key header so a retry cannot create a duplicate. Authentication​ OAuth 2.0: OAuth2ClientCredentials OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow. Tokens expire after 3600 seconds; cache the token and refresh it before it expires. Security Scheme Type: oauth2 OAuth Flow (clientCredentials): Token URL: https://auth.dzenterprise.io/oauth/token Scopes: api:read: Read any resource the client is entitled to see. api:write: Create, update, and delete resources. AI has become a permanent part of modern documentation workflows, and for good reason. It speeds up research, watches your wording, improves consistency, and helps teams move faster without giving up quality. Used well, AI is an extra pair of hands and an extra pair of eyes: it lets writers and managers spend less time on repetitive work and more time on real business problems. I have used these tools extensively over the past few years, but I have never handed them the reins. Claude helped with sandbox code analysis, troubleshooting, and automated testing. ChatGPT helped me check unfamiliar fintech concepts and international regulations. Grammarly caught typos and polished wording. They saved time and improved throughput, but they never owned the outcome. Every result was reviewed, challenged, and adapted to what the product and its users actually needed. In my experience, effective AI adoption rests on three principles: Competence, Caution, and Control.

documents.t: Competence comes first. There is a growing misconception that AI can compensate for a lack of expertise. It cannot. Access to a powerful model does not make anyone a technical writer, an engineer, or a product manager. If anything, the opposite is true: the less experience you have, the harder it is to spot an inaccuracy, a weak assumption, or an answer that is confidently wrong. AI produces its best work when it is guided by someone who already understands the domain, the product, and the expected outcome.

Caution matters just as much. Every prompt carries information, and information has value. Documentation teams work with proprietary business logic, customer data, and internal processes every day. Before you share anything with a model, know exactly what you are disclosing. Hoping the data will not leak is not a data-protection strategy. Corporate knowledge belongs inside the perimeter, not in a conversation with an external system. AI should protect the business, not expose it.

Finally, control. AI should be built into a workflow deliberately, not left to reshape that workflow on its own. For all its capability, a model has no judgment, no context, and no accountability. It can misread requirements, invent facts, miss edge cases, or produce something that reads convincingly and is fundamentally wrong. Responsibility for quality stays with the people running the system. Competent, cautious professionals set the rules, draw the boundaries, validate the output, and keep refining the process. That is how an organization gets the most out of AI while carrying the least risk. The teams that get the most from AI are not the ones chasing full automation. They are the ones that pair the technology with expertise and discipline. AI can sharpen the blade; it still takes a skilled hand to wield it. P.S. Practising what I preach: the first draft of this article was written with an LLM, from my outline and my arguments. What you just read is the version that survived my editing. That distinction is the whole point. A model can produce a draft in seconds; knowing what to keep, what to challenge, and what to rewrite is where professional experience earns its value.

documents.t: When I was promoted to Team Lead in 2021, I faced a challenge familiar to many first-time managers: how do you balance leadership responsibilities with your own day-to-day work without becoming a bottleneck? Management took roughly 20–30% of my time. I spent it building a sustainable documentation operation rather than supervising people. We introduced DITA-based practices in our XML-driven MadCap Flare environment, standardized terminology and writing conventions, and established quarterly quality reviews. Most importantly, I wanted the team to improve continuously while maintaining ownership of their work.
documents.s: Being an Effective Team Lead: Becoming a Force Multiplier

documents.t: My leadership philosophy was simple: technical writers are professionals, not content-producing machines. Reviews should highlight opportunities for improvement rather than dwell on mistakes. When people feel trusted and supported, they are far more likely to raise their own standards. One example: a writer whose drafts routinely needed several review cycles because of typos and inaccuracies in business examples. Instead of focusing on the symptoms, we addressed the process. I introduced a simple workflow diagram with an additional self-review step, encouraged earlier preparation of business examples during planning, and introduced Grammarly as a final quality check. The fix was simple and it worked. The writer spent slightly more time reviewing drafts before submission, and the number of review cycles dropped sharply. Documentation quality improved, reviewers regained valuable time, and the writer became more consistent because fewer documents were returned for rework.
documents.s: Being a leader is simple, being an effective leader is hard

documents.t: The real test came in 2022 when I had to rebuild the documentation team after the company's relocation to the United Kingdom. Different people, the same principles: clear workflows, professional standards, continuous improvement, and respect for the people behind the process. Within six months, the team's output increased fourfold compared to the early stages of rebuilding. Looking back, I learned that effective leadership is not about personally solving every problem. It is about creating an environment where talented people can do their best work. Strong processes matter. Quality standards matter. But the real multiplier is a team that trusts the workflow, trusts its leader, and takes pride in the result.

Browse GitHub long enough and you notice something: almost every repository has a README, yet comprehensive guides are rare. The reason is simple. The primary goal of documentation is to educate people about a product: what it does, why it exists, how to use it efficiently, how to avoid mistakes, and how to get the most value from it. Creating good documentation requires time, effort, discipline, and a genuine desire to help others succeed with your product. Those who neglect documentation usually have other priorities, and educating users is not one of them. In the enterprise world, however, documentation is not optional. Whether we're talking about Fintech platforms, treasury systems, SaaS products, or enterprise software in general, documentation is one of the foundations upon which customer success is built. Consider a simple analogy. When you buy a sophisticated piece of equipment — a coffee machine, a boiler, some new home electronics — you usually open the manual first, for two obvious reasons. You don't want to break something expensive by trial and error, and you want to start using it properly as fast as possible. Customers of a fintech product want exactly the same two things. They do not want to lose money, and they want to get more value out of what they bought. Good documentation serves both. Customers can judge the maturity of a product from the quality of its documentation alone. The line between good and bad documentation is obvious to any reader, and remarkably hard to cross. In my experience, great documentation rests on three pillars: integrity, actionability, and beauty.
documents.s: Integrity, Actionability, and Beauty: The Three Pillars of Great Documentation

documents.t: This one almost goes without saying. If your documentation states something incorrect, omits a critical detail, or misleads the reader, your credibility is gone. Integrity does not happen by accident. It takes continuous research, attention to detail, close work with subject-matter experts, a seat in testing, thorough reviews, and the ability to fix an issue before it reaches a customer. Integrity is what an efficient workflow produces. Clients rarely notice accurate documentation; they simply expect it. Inaccurate documentation they notice instantly — and then they start thinking about adding an “ex-” to the word “client”. Trust is far harder to win back than to keep.

Technical documentation is not a novel. Nobody opens a knowledge base for entertainment. People arrive with a problem and expect to leave with a solution. The best documentation respects the reader's time: focused, practical, built to get someone to a specific goal with minimal effort. No one wants to wade through a dozen paragraphs of background to reach the one step they actually needed. This is where empathy becomes one of the most valuable skills a technical writer has. A strong writer reads their own documentation through the customer's eyes and keeps finding the friction: the unclear explanation, the missing example, the complexity that earns nothing.

I deliberately use the word "beauty" instead of "clear interface" or "intuitive design" because true beauty in documentation encompasses all of those things and then some. An exceptional knowledge base is beautifully structured, beautifully written, beautifully designed, and beautifully delivered. Readers know instinctively where to go. They find answers quickly. Navigation feels natural, and the whole experience feels effortless. Beauty here is not decoration; it is a competitive advantage. Many companies treat documentation as a compliance checkbox: nobody really cares about it, but it has to exist because customers expect it to. The winners treat knowledge differently. They understand that documentation is part of the product experience. When users interact with your knowledge base, they are still interacting with your product, just through a different interface or access point.

These three principles do not cover the whole discipline. Documentation also depends on maintenance, stakeholder collaboration, governance, localization, analytics, and now AI-assisted workflows. But without integrity, actionability, and beauty, everything else is built on sand. One last analogy. Imagine sitting through a product presentation for a solution you are considering buying. The lights dim. The screen comes alive. The presenter walks on stage. They greet the room, and get straight to the point. They show the features that matter, walk through practical use cases, answer every question, and never waste a minute of your time. The talk is clear, engaging, and effortless to follow — and everything around it, from the slides to the pacing to the room itself, is considered. By the end you want the product, and you trust the people behind it. Exceptional documentation creates the same effect. It becomes the place customers go first, because experience has taught them that the answer is there and it is right. When documentation reaches that level, your support team runs into the most pleasant problem there is: There are very few tickets left to resolve.

This section presents documentation I wrote for the Hazeltree platform as a Senior Technical Writer. The samples come from several product modules and cover the range of documentation types that enterprise users and implementation teams rely on: knowledge base guides, product overviews, getting-started articles, and step-by-step implementation instructions. Each one takes a different approach to the same underlying problem — presenting complex functionality so that a reader can act on it. Confidentiality Notice Hazeltree's confidentiality requirements limit how much business and product context these samples can carry. Company-specific information and sensitive implementation details have been removed, blurred, anonymized, or generalized. The samples still preserve the original structure, writing style, and technical depth.

Format Knowledge base article examining the Algorithmic Reconciliation process at the core of the Reconciliation Manager module. Target Readers Quantitative analysts, financial data engineers, portfolio risk managers, and fund accountants. Description Original internal research and analysis of a company-developed self-learning engine algorithm, demonstrating how it reconciles Security entities across multiple data sources using Fuzzy logic. Business Impact Used by hedge funds and banking accounting systems for daily reference data accuracy. Critical for collateral management, loan positions, cashflows, and projected portfolios. Contributed to a 70% increase in module sales.

Reconciliation Manager is an administrative dashboard that helps confirm portfolio elements against counterparties and accounting systems. It enables clients to manage portfolio figures and ensure accurate reconciliation to mitigate operational risks and errors. Reconciliation Manager offers two data reconciliation solutions: Classic and Algorithmic. This Guide provides user instructions and explains the working principles of Algorithmic Recon. TermAlgorithmic Recon A data reconciliation engine based on Fuzzy logic. The Algorithmic Recon engine is a machine-learning background process that uses a special algorithm to calculate certainty and identify the best entity match based on reconciliation history. TermFuzzy logic A form of probability theory that calculates "degrees of truth" rather than the usual "true or false" Boolean logic. It addresses partial truth, where the truth value may range between completely true and completely false. Fuzzy logic is used in many fields, such as artificial intelligence. In the Algorithmic Recon, it powers the machine-learning process at the core of the engine. Security Recon runs in two phases: ID-Based Recon and Algorithmic Recon. ID-Based Recon runs first and processes only Listed Securities and Equity Swaps. Algorithmic Recon runs second and covers all Securities, including those not matched during the first phase. This document describes the second phase: Algorithmic Recon. Security Analysis: retains Securities with Strong, Weak, Potential, and Ambiguous map types assigned as a result of Security Algorithmic Recon. Not Mapped Securities: contains Securities not included in any Positions’ search spaces for the Algorithmic reconciliation process. Reinforcement Learning: contains and analyzes Algorithmic Recon data in a matrix table. Rejected Mappings: contains Security mappings from the Weak certainty group that users rejected on the Security Analysis screen. INFORMATION The Security Mappings screen in the ID-Based Security Recon toolbox is also considered part of Algorithmic Recon because it aggregates all extracted Securities mapped to system Securities (using both ID-Based and Algorithmic methods).

Security Algorithmic Recon, built on Fuzzy logic, follows a working principle different from Classic Security Recon. Security entities are extracted from the HUB_POSN and HUB_MRGD files (which contain Position records). The matching algorithm consists of the following steps: Step 1: Search space formation​ The search space is formed for Positions on the left side (House-side entities) and on the right side (Counterparty feed files). When Positions are extracted from the HUB_POSN and HUB_MRGD feed files, a search space is created for each right-side Position (Counterparty feed file). The search space is a pool of possible matches selected by the parameters Account, Direction, and Settlement Date. A Cartesian join method is used for this step. Click on the image below to expand it: Positions A, B, and C are candidates for collation on the House side because their basic parameters match. This forms the search space for Fuzzy logic reconciliation. The Algorithmic Recon Fuzzy engine then determines which candidate is the correct match. Positions with expired Securities (past their Maturity or Expiry date) do not participate in reconciliation and are excluded from the search space in the first step of the algorithm. INFORMATION It is common for a House Position to be split into several Positions for business or planning purposes (for example, by Position strategy). In that case, multiple House Positions may be matched to a single Counterparty Position (for example, in bank reports). The matching routine proceeds in the same way as regular one-to-one matching. Step 2: Pair Similarity calculation​ Pair Similarity calculation is performed for Positions within the search space, using three Predicates for a specific group of fields and the selected Strategy. To determine the correct candidate, the Algorithmic Recon engine calculates the Pair Similarity value. This value is assembled from three Predicates computed for each candidate. TermPredicate A calculated variable that represents the matching strength of Position and Security entities and is used to compute the Pair Similarity value. Predicates are based on the matching fields of reconciled right-side and left-side Position items. Algorithmic Recon uses three Predicates: Position required fields (Quantity and Market Value Local), Security description fields (ISIN, CUSIP, Underlying Security, Issuer, Description, etc.), and Position additional fields (Market Value Book, Price Local, FX Rate, Daily Accrual Basis, etc.). Position required fields have the highest weight at 0.4, Security description fields have a weight of 0.35, and Position additional fields have the lowest weight at 0.25. Together, the three Predicates sum to a total weight of 1. Therefore, the algorithm scans the fields of the Counterparty Position and House Position candidates, starting with the most important fields: Quantity and Market Value Local, which form the first Predicate target group (Position required fields). Values may be missing on one side of the comparison. For example, the House Position may have the ISIN field populated while the Counterparty file does not (or vice versa). In these cases, the Fuzzy engine applies the Recon Missing Values Strategy. TermRecon Missing Values Strategy A two-way method used during field collation when compared Positions lack a value on one side but have it on the other. When the Recon Strategy is set to Optimistic, the system assumes the missing value matches the value on the opposite side, which adds points to the computed Predicate. When the Recon Strategy is set to Pessimistic, the system assumes the missing value does not match the value on the opposite side, which subtracts points from the Predicate. INFORMATION When both sides lack data in the compared field, the Recon Strategy is not applied and does not affect the Predicate result. Click the image below to see the complete Algorithmic reconciliation workflow schema: CRITICAL FAILURE IN FIELDS COMPARISON The second Predicate, Security description fields, includes fields that compare the Securities attributes of Positions on opposite sides. These fields are grouped into two sets: Required and Sufficient. Required is a group of highly critical values (Security Type, Currency Code, Effective Date, Strike Price, Underlying SEDOL, Underlying CUSIP, Underlying ISIN). If values in these fields do not match, the Predicate’s weight decreases sharply, which reduces the chance of a match. If they do match, the weight increases slightly. Sufficient is a group of values with lower criticality (SEDOL, CUSIP, ISIN, Ticket, RIC, and Security Code). These fields may legitimately differ for the same Security. For Sufficient fields, a match drives a sharp increase in weight, while a discrepancy causes a sharp decrease. When all three Predicates are calculated, the Pair Similarity value is assembled for each candidate. Pair Similarity ranges from zero to one hundred, where zero indicates a complete mismatch across all Position and Security fields and one hundred indicates a perfect match across all fields. In general, each mismatch subtracts points from the Predicate. It is unlikely that all Predicates will achieve the full combined weight of 1. As a result, Pair Similarity works like a competition: the highest-scoring candidate is selected to match with the House Security. See the example below. ExamplePredicates calculation The incoming Broker Report from the HUB_POSN file contains thousands of records, and each one undergoes the Algorithmic Recon procedure. Here is an example of a single record retrieved from HUB_POSN to find its match among the entities on the company side: Based on the search space formed using the Position parameters (Account, Direction, and Settlement Date), there are four candidates for the right-side Security with the appropriate Security Map Type. Pair Similarity is then calculated for each candidate: GLTUK2022: has only one matching Security Description field. Pair Similarity is computed as 13% probability. GLTUK-RA: has three matching fields, one of which adds points to the Position required fields Predicate. In addition, the critical values in the second Security description field Predicate match. Pair Similarity is computed at 76% probability. GL-T-UK22: also has three matching fields, but none align with the highest-weighted Predicate. Pair Similarity is computed at 59% probability. GTU: this candidate has the lowest Pair Similarity at 0 percent probability, since no fields match on the right side. In this reconciliation round, GLTUK-RA scores the highest Pair Similarity and is therefore mapped to the right-side Security. However, whether the mapping is automatically approved, requires user approval, or is classified as a potential map is determined in the third step of the reconciliation process. Step 3: Best Pair selection​ Based on the calculated Pair Similarity value, the system selects the best Securities for mapping. Position matching based on the highest Pair Similarity leads to a key step in Security Recon: matching Securities within Positions. Securities inherit the Pair Similarity score of their Positions. This Security Pair Similarity determines the mapping strength applied in step 4. The Pair Similarity for Positions (and for Position Securities) is calculated using the engine logic described in Step 2. Step 4: Mapping Strength​ The system determines the mapping strength for the best Pair Similarity scorer, based on the Confidence Level and Distance. After the engine identifies the winner of the matching contest, it determines the mapping strength. There are four possible mapping strengths: Strong: high accuracy, mapping is created automatically. Weak: decent accuracy, mapping is created but requires the user’s approval. Potential: low accuracy, mapping is automatically added to the Candidates list and can be reviewed; mappings can then be created manually. Ambiguous: undecided mapping, since the Pair Similarity of matching candidates is identical; in this case, the mapping conflict must be resolved manually by a user. The engine determines the mapping strength based on two parameters (Confidence Level and Distance) and their ratio within the Reinforcement Learning matrix. TermConfidence Level Mapping certainty value. This value is taken directly from the calculated Pair Similarity of the reconciliation winner. The higher the Confidence Level, the stronger the mapping. TermDistance Difference between the Pair Similarities of the reconciliation winner and the second-place candidate. The greater the difference between the winner and the closest competitor, the higher the certainty of the mapping. If there is only one candidate in the search space, the Distance equals the Confidence Level. Confidence Level and Distance form the axes of the Reinforcement Learning matrix table. The matrix table is available on the [Reinforcement Learning screen] (#reinforcement-screen). TermReinforcement Learning matrix table A dynamic, self-modifying table. Columns represent Confidence Level ranges and rows represent Distance ranges. The system calculates these ranges from the full set of Algorithmic mappings: the more mappings that exist across different Confidence Levels and Distances, the narrower each range becomes. IMPORTANT The position of a new mapping on the matrix table determines its strength: landing in a green cell defines a Strong mapping, landing in a yellow cell defines a Weak mapping, and landing in a white cell grants a Potential status. Ambiguous mappings are not considered in the matrix table unless the mapping conflict is resolved manually by a user. The Reinforcement matrix table is shown in the screenshot below. Click to expand: SELF-LEARNING MECHANISM OF THE ALGORITHMIC RECON ENGINE In an ideal situation, with equal proportions of reconciled data and no discrepancies or user corrections, the ratio of the Strong/Weak/Potential zones in the Reinforcement Learning matrix table would be approximately as follows: Indeed, the smaller the difference in Pair Similarity between a low-Confidence Level winner and the second-place candidate, the higher the odds of an erroneous mapping. By contrast, the higher the Confidence Level and the larger the gap between Pair Similarities, the smaller the margin for error. In practice, mismappings occur across different Confidence Levels and Distances, so the strength ratio within the Reinforcement Learning matrix is constantly changing. For example, when a user finds an error in a Strong mapping and corrects it, the green Strong cell where the mapping landed is downgraded to Weak or Potential. As a result, the final decision on mapping strength depends on a self-learning mechanism that adapts dynamically to mapping history and user corrections. The more entities are mapped, the more mappings are confirmed, and the more errors are corrected manually, the smarter the Fuzzy engine becomes. The Reinforcement Learning screen allows users to dive deep into mapping statistics, review mapping Pair Similarities and Predicates at different levels, and analyze mappings alongside the Fuzzy engine. Step 5: Reconciliation results​ The system populates the Security Mappings, Security Analysis, and Not Mapped Securities screens with the Algorithmic Recon results for every reconciled Security entity. In the Algorithmic Recon final phase, the system populates the screen grids with reconciliation results. There are three resultant screens of Security Algorithmic Recon: Security Mappings: an aggregation screen that shows all mappings and mapping suggestions in the system for a designated period. Security Analysis: an operational analysis screen that contains mapped and not-mapped Securities, and allows users to create, approve, reject, and break mappings. Not Mapped Securities: an aggregation screen that contains only not-mapped Securities, allowing users to review and manually map entities that have no mappings. Once the results are written to the system, users can begin reviewing Security mappings, approving Weak mappings, creating Potential mappings, and correcting errors. ROLL-UP ACCOUNT IN SECURITY POSITIONS You can configure the system to check whether Security Positions have Accounts with assigned Roll-up Accounts. To activate this check during Algorithmic Recon, set the Company Preference HubRecon - Aggregate Positions On Rollup Account to True: If activated, reconciled Security Positions will show Roll-up Accounts instead of the main Account on the resultant Security Analysis screen. NOTE: Activating this Company Preference also impacts the Classic Position Recon process in the same way.
