Format Knowledge base guide combining an explanation of algorithmic transaction matching principles with a practical user guide for the Transaction Matching module. Target Readers Reconciliation analysts, operations analysts, accountants, and financial operations specialists responsible for validating and resolving transaction discrepancies. Description Technical reference and onboarding guide explaining the scientific principles behind algorithmic transaction matching across heterogeneous data sources. Also provides a complete walkthrough of the Transaction Matching interface supported by real-world reconciliation scenarios and live case examples. Business Impact Served as the primary reference for six of the company's largest reconciliation clients, improving adoption of advanced transaction matching workflows and reducing analyst onboarding time. The documentation also supported customer enablement efforts that contributed to two existing clients purchasing the Reconciliation Manager module.

Transaction Matching is a critical step of the Transaction Reconciliation process. It matches Transaction records between the House side (Company) and the Counterparty side (Broker, Bank, or Accounting system). The Algorithmic Transaction Matching process runs on Hazeltree's in-house engine, built on Fuzzy logic at its core. ALGORITHMIC TRANSACTION MATCHING PROCESS Comparing Transactions from two sources — House and Counterparty — with Fuzzy logic gives customers control over the integrity of real asset movements. Financial operations wired through multiple institutions vary too widely for exact matching, which is why the Fuzzy logic engine exists. Consider a set of international Transactions. The assets pass through intermediary banks before they reach the receiving Account, and the client needs to know which Transactions have settled and which are still in flight. The bank produces report files covering the day's operations and sends them to the client. Hazeltree processes those files and compares the extracted data with the House data. The client then sees the full picture: what has completed, and what is still to come. The self-learning Algorithmic engine streamlines Transaction matching and reduces the risk of an incorrect match, giving clients fast and dependable results. ExampleAlgorithmic Transaction Matching in a Private Equity deal Algorithmic Transaction Matching is best illustrated through a Private Equity scenario. A client issues an Investor Call letter and creates a Voucher with multiple Transactions from the posted Cashflow Transfers. Naturally, the client needs to track the incoming investments until the call is fulfilled, and such investments usually take time to be agreed on and wired. The Transaction Matching screen gives the client a single control point for monitoring the steady stream of incoming investment Transactions. Because the number of incoming Transactions can be large and their settlement timing varies, the client delegates Transaction comparison and matching to the Fuzzy engine. The user's job is to verify the integrity of the matching process and analyze the results. Once the final Transactions are wired and reported, the client can confirm whether everything was transferred as planned, or whether there are discrepancies to raise with the investors.

The Algorithmic Transaction Matching process combines several approaches that improve accuracy and integrity. It is a multi-step procedure, shown in the diagram below: Input: the Fuzzy algorithm starts with the full set of Transactions that participate in the algorithmic matching process. This set is assembled on the Transaction Matching screen when the user starts Algorithmic Matching. Fuzzy Transaction Matching: the process runs in two parallel modes — 1:1 Matching and M:N Matching. 1:1 relations: relations are established between a single right-side Transaction (Broker) and a single left-side Transaction (House). This mode is called One-To-One and is based on the calculated Confidence Level. M:N relations: relations are established among right-side Transactions (Broker) and left-side Transactions (House). This mode is called Many-To-Many and works in several combinations (Many-To-One, One-To-Many, and Many-To-Many). Matching in this mode is based on the Reference Number ID. Cross-group link identification: an auxiliary step of the M:N relations that looks for possible matches among the individual Transactions in the groups formed by M:N matching. The search is based on the Reference Number ID. Cross-group relations: cross-group matches are established. As a result, a single Transaction can belong to two or more subgroups (for example, when it carries multiple Reference Number IDs in the Description field). Subgroups merge: the subgroups formed by M:N mode are fused through a 1:1 match established between members of different groups. This mode is called Cross Grouping through 1:1 Matching. Output: the resulting groups are displayed on the Transaction Matching grid with their calculated Confidence Levels. Because Transaction records are held differently across accounting institutions, the Transaction Matching process runs in three modes: One-To-One — one Transaction to one Transaction. M:N Matching, with three variations: One-To-Many — one Transaction to many Transactions. Many-To-One — many Transactions to one Transaction. Many-To-Many — many Transactions to many Transactions. Cross Grouping through 1:1 Matching — Many-To-Many groups linked through a One-To-One match and an established cross-group connection. These different approaches exist because the number of Transaction records can differ between the House and Counterparty sides. NOTE The One-To-One mode follows a dedicated algorithm that involves forming a search space. The One-To-Many, Many-To-One, and Many-To-Many modes are special cases of M:N matching, which follows a separate algorithm based on finding and matching Transactions by their Reference Number. Both matching processes run in parallel, with neither taking priority. Cross Grouping runs after the 1:1 and M:N matching processes finish.
One-To-One Transaction Matching connects one Transaction from the House side to one Transaction from the Counterparty side. It is the simplest matching case, and the process proceeds as follows:

A search space is formed for the ungrouped Transactions from the left side (House) and the right side (Counterparty). TermSearch space A set of right-side and left-side Transactions that participate in the Algorithmic Matching process. Before the process starts, the search space is filtered: Transactions with the Vetted status and Transaction groups are excluded. INFORMATION Once the search space is formed, the right-side and left-side Transactions are multiplied using the Cross Join method (every right-side Transaction is compared with every left-side Transaction). To optimize the process and avoid server memory overload, the Cross Join method compares a set of parameters: Currency, Amount, Settlement Date, and Trade Date. The Amount, Settlement Date, and Trade Date parameters have configurable thresholds that widen the room for matching. These thresholds are configured through Company Preferences. Launching Algorithmic Matching​ Transaction data is loaded by the regular Sync Manager process, Client Writer Update. By default, this process is launched by Sync Manager according to the Sync Manager Scheduler. It takes all Transactions from the House and Counterparty sides for a period of T-30 days (today minus thirty). INFORMATION Users can also re-run Algorithmic Matching from the Hazeltree interface and set the coverage period manually. On the Transaction Matching screen, set the following Upper toolbar filters before starting Algorithmic Matching: Date Type (Trade Date or Settlement Date) Date From Date To Once these parameters are set, the Transactions appear on the grid. To launch the Fuzzy logic engine, click Reprocess. Forming the search space from the full set of Transactions is unique to One-To-One mode; it does not apply to M:N mode. All manually ungrouped Transactions (those removed from groups by users) are excluded from matching in later iterations of Algorithmic Matching. The system seeks new pairs and leaves the ungrouped Transactions out of the pool of candidates. A Transaction's ungrouped state is marked in a dedicated column on the Transaction Matching screen: Is Ungrouped.

Pair Similarity is calculated for the Transactions inside the search space using three Predicates for particular field groups. A search space can contain multiple matching candidates, so to decide which candidate is correct, the Recon engine calculates Pair Similarity. This value is assembled from three Predicates computed for every candidate. TermPredicate A variable representing Transaction matching strength, used to compute Pair Similarity. Predicates are based on the matching fields of the reconciled right-side (Counterparty) and left-side (House) Transactions. The Algorithmic Transaction Matching process uses three Predicates: Main qualitative required features (Trade Date, Settlement Date, Currency, Security, Account, Portfolio), Main quantitative required features (Quantity, Net Amount Local, Market Value Book, Notional Net Amount), and Additional natural-language fuzzy features (Description, Type). Main qualitative required features carry the heaviest weight, 0.4; Main quantitative required features carry a lighter weight, 0.35; and Additional natural-language fuzzy features carry the lightest weight, 0.25. All Predicate weights are dynamic and can range between zero and their maximum value. In an ideal case, when all three Predicates reach their maximum during this step, they add up to a total weight of 1. INFORMATION The Fuzzy engine uses a special system column that holds a cumulative description of the internal Transaction's Cashflow, which is compared with the data received from the Counterparty side. This system field is not visible in the Hazeltree interface. It contains the following parameters: Cashflow Name, Legal Entity, Investment, Investor (with their text UDFs), Cashflow Description, and Transfer Name. ENTROPY (INFORMATION THEORY) IN MATCHING PROCESS During the Predicates’ weight calculation, the Algorithmic Matching process compares the left and right Transactions’ Quantities (Main quantitative required features group), and this is where the Fuzzy engine uses the principle of Entropy (information theory). In the information theory the entropy is a concept that tells how much information there is in a certain event (in our case, in the Transactions comparison). In general, the more certain or deterministic the comparison is, the less information it needs. Therefore, the comparison of the Quantity values of both Transactions can either increase or decrease in the entropy. Example 1: the Quantity of both Transactions is $100,000,000.00. The uncertainty increases, since such flat Quantity can be not unique in the Search space that contains a lot of Transactions. The weight calculated for the Main quantitative required features will decrease. Example 2: the Quantity of both Transactions is $98,104,637.89. The uncertainty decreases, since such number diverse Quantity is most certainly unique in the Search space. The weight calculated for the Main quantitative required features will increase.

Based on the calculated Pair Similarity, the algorithm selects the best Transactions to map. The computed Pair Similarities are compared, and the winner is matched. The winner's Pair Similarity becomes the Confidence Level (the mapping certainty value). Based on the Confidence Level, the algorithm decides whether the Transactions should be grouped automatically on the Transaction Matching screen.

Reconciled Transactions are grouped on the grid. Using the winner's Confidence Level, the Fuzzy logic algorithm decides whether the Transactions should be grouped automatically or require manual approval. To do this, it compares the calculated Confidence Level with the system value Min Confidence Level: Confidence Level of 100%: the two matching Transactions have identical Accounts, Amounts, Settlement Dates, Reference Numbers, and Currencies. The algorithm matches and groups the Transactions automatically. Below 100% but above the Min Confidence Level: the algorithm matches and groups the Transactions automatically. Below the Min Confidence Level but with the same Reference Numbers in the Description or Notes fields: the algorithm groups the Transactions automatically and sets the Require Approval indicator. It does not match the Transactions automatically. INFORMATION The Algorithmic Transaction Matching process also considers the Payee Codes and Payee Names in the Transaction Description field. ExampleOne-To-One matching In 1:1 mode, the engine forms a search space for the House-side Transaction and calculates the most accurate pair from the sum of three Predicates that analyze the matching fields. Once the connection between the two Transactions is established, they are grouped and displayed on the Transaction Matching screen: Grouped Transactions: the group of Transactions matched in 1:1 mode. The group Status is Matched, and the Description shows the details of the matching process. Expanded group with details: the user can expand the group and review the Transactions matched during the Algorithmic process. If the match was erroneous, the user can manually ungroup the cluster, which excludes the ungrouped pair from the search space in subsequent iterations of Algorithmic Matching.

M:N Transaction Matching applies when the number of matched entities differs between the House and Counterparty records. To connect the Transaction records correctly, the Fuzzy engine relies on the Reference Number value. TermReference Number A unique numeric identifier assigned to a financial Transaction. It is generated by the system and tied to a single Transaction, helping an institution identify Transactions in its records and databases. In the Transaction matching process, the Reference Number is a strong anchor that helps identify all interlinked Transactions from the House and Counterparty sides and match them accurately. When searching for a Reference Number, the Fuzzy algorithm scans two fields: the Reference Number field and the Transaction Description. M:N mode has three variations: One Transaction to many Transactions (One-To-Many) Many Transactions to one Transaction (Many-To-One) Many Transactions to many Transactions (Many-To-Many) NOTE This mode does not build a search space of one or several matching candidates. Instead, all Transactions in the algorithmic matching process form the search space. The algorithm assumes there can be an unlimited number of money transfers (additional Transactions, difference returns, corrections, and so on).

One-To-Many Transaction Matching connects one Transaction from the House side to several Transactions from the Counterparty side. It covers cases where a single House-side Transaction stands for several Counterparty-side Transactions. ExampleOne-To-Many matching The House Transaction shows a cash movement of $266,596,105 settled on 10/8/2022. The Counterparty shows three Transactions: a cash movement of $266,373,400, a cash movement of $1,290, and a cash movement of $221,415. In reality, the first Transaction moved $222,705 less than required, and the shortfall was later transferred in two portions because of an accountant's miscalculation. In Hazeltree, only one Transaction was created to represent this cash movement. During algorithmic matching, the three Counterparty Transactions should be matched to the single House Transaction. The Fuzzy algorithm searches for the Transaction Reference ID in the Ref ID and Description fields. The match can be Strong (Confidence Level of 100%) or Weak (Confidence Level below 100%). The House Transaction is matched to the three Counterparty Transactions using the Reference Number ID MONSTSTHK125101IHRA2B5S, found in the Transaction Ref ID field (for the primary Transaction with the incorrect Amount) and the Description field (for the two complementary Transactions). The Transaction Matching screen then displays the group: Grouped Transactions: the group of Transactions matched in M:N mode. The group Status is Matched, and the Description shows the details of the matching process. Expanded group with details: the same group, expanded to show each matched Transaction and its Confidence Level.

Many-To-One Transaction Matching connects several Transactions from the House side to one Transaction from the Counterparty side. It covers cases where multiple House-side Transactions stand for a single Counterparty-side Transaction. INFORMATION This is a special case where several Transactions are created in Hazeltree under one Voucher, all sharing the same Transaction Reference Number (inherited from the Voucher). The Counterparty side sends a single wire for the sum of all Transactions in the Voucher and reports the Voucher's Reference Number. The Fuzzy logic then groups the Hazeltree Transactions with the single Broker wire based on the identical Reference Number.

Many-To-Many Transaction Matching connects several Transactions from the House side to several Transactions from the Counterparty side. It covers cases where multiple House-side Transactions stand for a set of multiple Counterparty-side Transactions. NOTE The number of House Transactions and Counterparty Transactions can differ (for example, four House Transactions matched to three Counterparty Transactions) or be equal. In either case, the matching process relies on the Reference Number value across the whole set of grouped Transactions. ExampleMany-To-Many matching The Many-To-Many case is the most common in Transaction Matching. To display all right-side Transactions matched to the set of left-side Transactions, expand the group and scroll its Transaction list. Grouped Transactions: the group of Transactions matched in M:N mode. The group Status is Matched, and the Description shows the details of the matching process. Expanded group with details: the same group, expanded to show every matched Transaction on both sides. The Many-To-Many case carries the highest risk of error because of the number of entities involved, especially early in the Fuzzy engine's self-learning process for a given client. To correct a Many-To-Many group manually, users can exclude the excess Transactions from it.

The Fuzzy logic of Transaction matching includes a special mode that extends the algorithm and adds precision. It is called Cross Grouping through 1:1 Matching. Cross Grouping works through an additional algorithm step in which one Transaction from an already formed group is matched with one Transaction from a different formed group. As a result, the two groups are merged into one. The Counterparty Transaction with ID 649130 is matched in M:N mode via the Transaction Reference Number (Ref ID) T320365BGH0. Under the Fuzzy logic of M:N matching, a matching Ref ID in the Transaction Reference ID field yields a Confidence Level of 100%. The Counterparty Transaction with ID 650085 is matched in M:N mode via the Ref ID T320365BGH0. Here the Ref ID was retrieved from the Transaction Description field, so the calculated Confidence Level is 95%. Transactions 649130 and 650085 are grouped as a Voucher from the Broker (Counterparty side). The House Transaction with ID 640951 is matched in M:N mode via the Ref ID 4714978. A matching Ref ID in the Transaction Reference ID field yields a Confidence Level of 100%. The House Transaction with ID 637179 is matched in M:N mode via the Ref ID 4714978. Again, a matching Ref ID in the Transaction Reference ID field yields a Confidence Level of 100%. Transactions 640951 and 637179 are grouped as a Voucher on the House side. During the parallel 1:1 matching process, Transaction 649130 (Counterparty side) and Transaction 640951 (House side) are matched on similar values in the following fields: Net Amount Local Currency Code Account Trade Date Settlement Date NOTE The calculated Confidence Level is 82%. The drop from 100% is caused by an unmatched Transaction Type field (the House-side field is empty). 82% is still enough for automatic matching, since it is below 100% but above the Min Confidence Level threshold. All Transactions are shown as one group on the Transaction Matching screen. If the automatic grouping through 1:1 Matching is erroneous, users can manually ungroup the Transactions on the Transaction Matching screen: IMPORTANT When a Transaction group created through Cross Grouping is ungrouped manually, the 1:1 connection between the two linking Transactions is broken and barred from future algorithmic matching. This connection is excluded from the search space for 1:1 Matching, and the system looks for a new pair. The M:N connections established before the Cross Grouping remain intact.

The Transaction Matching screen is the result screen of the Algorithmic Matching reconciliation process. It displays the Transaction groups formed by the Fuzzy engine, along with the single Transactions that remain unmatched. Upper toolbar filters: filters that narrow the Transactions shown on the grid. Upper toolbar buttons: operational buttons for working with the Transaction entities on the grid (Reprocess, Group, Vet, Merge, Create Internal Transaction). Grid: the list of Transactions (Grouped, Internal, and External) for the selected period. Context menu: the options available for the selected Transaction or Transactions. INFORMATION The Transaction Matching screen provides tools that let users control the Algorithmic Matching process: Grouping, Vetting, and Merging.

Group Transactions is a context-menu option that appears when two or more Transactions are selected on the grid. It combines the Transactions into a single group. When clicked, it opens the Transaction Group Editor in a pop-up window that shows the selected Transactions from the House side and the Counterparty side. Here you can add a Status, Tags, Business Status, and Description to the group. INFORMATION The Transaction Group Editor is also used to edit Transaction Groups — for example, to exclude incorrectly added Transactions. The editor is described below: General group settings: the Group Name, Status, Business Status, and Tags parameters. Internal: the collection of House-side (Internal) Transactions matched with the External Transactions. The sub-grid shows the Confidence Level from the Algorithmic Matching results and other system parameters (Vet status, Group status). External: the collection of Counterparty-side (External) Transactions matched with the Internal Transactions. The sub-grid shows the Confidence Level from the Algorithmic Matching results and other system parameters (Vet status, Group status). Description: a note field for adding commentary about the nature of the group and the technical details of how it was formed. INFORMATION Status and Business Status are different parameters of the Transaction Group. The Status field shows the state of matching progress (Matched, Partially Matched, Unmatched, Other). Business Status is a customizable value that shows additional information about the group (Awaiting More Transactions, Free to Edit, and so on). Business Status values are customized through the Dictionaries tool in the Reference Data module.

Vet Transactions and Transaction Groups is an option that lets users flag entities as Vetted (that is, checked). Once a Transaction or Transaction Group is vetted, it no longer participates in subsequent iterations of the Algorithmic Matching process. INFORMATION This option lets users regulate how many entities go through the Algorithmic Matching procedure. When the Vet status is removed from Transactions, they immediately become candidates again for the next iterations of the process.

The Merge Transaction Groups option lets users manually combine formed Transaction Groups into a single unit. This context-menu option appears when two or more Transaction Groups are selected on the grid.

Algorithmic Transaction Matching uses a self-learning Fuzzy engine that improves its accuracy with every iteration by analyzing the processed data and manual corrections. Fuzzy matching precision is further improved by custom tags assigned to Transactions. These tags, called Transaction Classifications, are created and managed on the Dictionaries screen (Reference Data module). Transaction Classification tags can be mapped to the Transaction attributes Transaction Code and Source. The mapping screen is opened with the context-menu option Add Transaction Classification Mapping: For example, a user maps the Transaction Classification S103_T to the Internal code (see the screenshot below). The Classification Code for this Transaction then takes the Internal value. If no mapping is found, the Classification Code field stays empty. INFORMATION Transaction Classification mapping has a positive effect on the Predicates calculated during 1:1 Matching, so the Confidence Level rises and matching becomes more reliable.
The samples in this portfolio come from a documentation system I designed and ran for eight years. This page explains that system. Good docs are not a writing effort, they're an operating process.

Docs start where users get stuck. I came to technical writing from five years in support and implementation. Every guide I write starts from a real failure point: a recurring ticket, a stalled onboarding, a misused feature, not from the system architecture. Documentation is a product. It has users, a roadmap, a backlog, releases, and success metrics. I ran it that way: prioritized by user impact, shipped on schedule, measured by outcomes. If it's done twice, automate it. Repetitive documentation work is a bug in the process.

The knowledge base I built at Hazeltree grew to 200+ guides across 18 product modules, and stayed navigable because the architecture was decided before the content: One structure for all modules. Every module followed the same pattern (overview, setup, workflows, reference, troubleshooting) so users who learned one module could navigate any other. Single source of truth. Shared concepts (glossary terms, common procedures, screenshots of shared UI) lived in one place and were reused, not copied. This pushed content reusability to ~80% and made global updates a one-file change. Layered depth. Each guide works at three reading depths: skim the headings, read the workflow, or descend into the reference tables, so the same document serves a new user and an expert.

Documentation lived in version control and moved like code: Author in Markdown, in a branch. Review is peer review for language and standards, SME review for technical accuracy, both as pull-request reviews with tracked comments. Merge and publish through the same pipeline every time, no manual uploads, no "final_v2" files. This gave the team full history, painless rollbacks, parallel work on the same doc set, and a review trail for every change.

Documentation shipped in lockstep with the product: 60+ releases over my tenure: Doc work was scoped during feature planning, not after code freeze. I sat in planning sessions with Product and Engineering, which also let me flag UX and naming issues before they shipped. Each release produced: updated guides, API reference updates, and release notes cross-linked to the relevant documentation (see the Release Notes sample). Release notes were generated by a Python pipeline I built, drawing on structured inputs from the tracker and AI-assisted drafting (Claude, Copilot) with human review. This roughly doubled delivery efficiency - the writers' time went to guides, not changelogs.

Support tickets were the feedback channel. Recurring questions became documentation tasks; documentation fixes were tracked against ticket volume. Over time, self-service documentation cut support workload by ~30%. Standards were written down. A living style guide covered terminology, screenshot conventions, and structure templates, which is what made review fast and the KB consistent across writers.

This page describes an automation script that streamlines the process of collecting TFS features, user stories, and bug fixes that form the basis of Release Notes documentation. The script is production-ready and has been successfully used to support the preparation of Release Notes.

Release Notes authoring in enterprise environments typically involves manually opening dozens of TFS work items and reviewing descriptions, comments, and discussion threads. When a release contains 50 to 80 items, this process can require several hours of repetitive navigation and analysis. The TFS Release Notes Extractor automates the information-gathering phase. It queries TFS using WIQL, iterates through all matching work items, and compiles relevant content into a single structured text file ready for review. As a result, collaboration with stakeholders can begin as soon as a release is announced, rather than after the manual collection process is complete. Manual extraction vs TFS Extractor script​ Manual process TFS Extractor Open each work item individually Single query fetches all items at once Copy-paste Description, Notes, Comments All fields extracted and structured automatically Risk of missing items or fields Query enforces consistent scope every time 8-14 hours per release cycle ~30 seconds to generate the raw file The generated output file becomes a single source of truth for the release cycle: a clean, readable document containing information about all release features, enhancements, and bug fixes. With a complete overview available immediately, it becomes easier to identify priorities and structure the Release Notes around the most significant changes.

The script filters work items by two conditions: Include in Release Notes: a checkbox that developers tick when a change is documentation-relevant Release Version: a field set to a version string such as 11.3 Only items matching both conditions are included in the output.

For every work item in the query, the script extracts and writes: Work item type, ID, and title Description: the full technical description of the change Release Notes: the developer-authored notes Comments: the full comment thread, numbered chronologically Before you start Save the script below as a file on your computer before running it. The commands in the How to Run section execute the saved file. They will not work if you paste the code directly into the terminal.

🐍 Python 🖥️ Bash Requirements pip install requests Save the script as tfs_release_notes.py, then run: python tfs_release_notes.py Before running, open the file and fill in the three stubs at the top: TFS_BASE_URL = "https://YOUR_TFS_SERVER/tfs/YOUR_COLLECTION/YOUR_PROJECT" RELEASE_VERSION = "11.3" PAT = "YOUR_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN" Requirements No installation needed. Uses only standard Unix tools: curl, sed, grep, base64. Save the script as tfs_release_notes.sh, make it executable, then run: chmod +x tfs_release_notes.sh ./tfs_release_notes.sh Before running, open the file and fill in the three stubs at the top: TFS_BASE_URL="https://YOUR_TFS_SERVER/tfs/YOUR_COLLECTION/YOUR_PROJECT" RELEASE_VERSION="11.3" PAT="YOUR_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN"

""" import os import requests from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth from datetime import datetime # Parameters to fill TFS_BASE_URL = "https://YOUR_TFS_SERVER/tfs/YOUR_COLLECTION/YOUR_PROJECT" #replace with TFS path RELEASE_VERSION = "11.3" #replace with release version OUTPUT_PATH = os.path.expanduser("~/Desktop/dz_release_notes.txt") # Personal Access Token (get from User Settings > Security) PAT = "YOUR_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN" # replace with PAT # TFS Query, WIQL (SQL-like syntax to form the query) WIQL_QUERY = f""" SELECT [System.Id], [System.Title], [System.WorkItemType] FROM WorkItems WHERE [System.TeamProject] = @project AND [System.WorkItemType] IN ('Feature', 'User Story', 'Bug') AND [Custom.IncludeInReleaseNotes] = True AND [Custom.ReleaseVersion] = '{RELEASE_VERSION}' ORDER BY [System.WorkItemType], [System.Id] """ # Helpers def tfs_get(endpoint: str) -> dict: """Send an authenticated GET request to the TFS REST API.""" url = f"{TFS_BASE_URL}/_apis/{endpoint}&api-version=5.0" response = requests.get(url, auth=HTTPBasicAuth("", PAT)) response.raise_for_status() return response.json() def run_wiql(query: str) -> list[int]: """Execute a WIQL query and return a list of matching work item IDs.""" url = f"{TFS_BASE_URL}/_apis/wit/wiql?api-version=5.0" payload = {"query": query} response = requests.post(url, json=payload, auth=HTTPBasicAuth("", PAT)) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() return [item["id"] for item in data.get("workItems", [])] def get_work_item(item_id: int) -> dict: """Fetch full details for a single work item by ID.""" url = ( f"{TFS_BASE_URL}/_apis/wit/workitems/{item_id}" f"?$expand=all&api-version=5.0" # $expand=all pulls in relations and comments alongside field values ) response = requests.get(url, auth=HTTPBasicAuth("", PAT)) response.raise_for_status() return response.json() def get_comments(item_id: int) -> list[str]: """Fetch all comments for a work item and return them as a list of strings.""" url = ( f"{TFS_BASE_URL}/_apis/wit/workitems/{item_id}/comments" f"?api-version=5.0-preview" ) response = requests.get(url, auth=HTTPBasicAuth("", PAT)) if response.status_code == 404: return [] response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() return [c.get("text", "").strip() for c in data.get("comments", []) if c.get("text")] def strip_html(text: str) -> str: """Remove HTML tags from rich-text fields (Description, Release Notes).""" import re if not text: return "" clean = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", text) clean = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", clean) return clean.strip() def format_item(item: dict, comments: list[str]) -> str: """Format a single work item into a readable text block.""" fields = item.get("fields", {}) item_id = item.get("id") item_type = fields.get("System.WorkItemType", "Unknown") title = fields.get("System.Title", "(no title)") description = strip_html(fields.get("System.Description", "")) release_notes = strip_html(fields.get("Custom.ReleaseNotes", "")) # NOTE: Custom.ReleaseNotes — replace with the actual reference name # for Release Notes field. lines = [ "=" * 72, f"[{item_type}] #{item_id} — {title}", "=" * 72, ] lines.append("
DESCRIPTION") lines.append("-" * 40) lines.append(description if description else "(empty)") lines.append("
RELEASE NOTES") lines.append("-" * 40) lines.append(release_notes if release_notes else "(empty)") lines.append("
COMMENTS") lines.append("-" * 40) if comments: for i, comment in enumerate(comments, start=1): lines.append(f"[{i}] {comment}") else: lines.append("(no comments)") lines.append("") # trailing blank line between items return "
".join(lines) # Script body def main(): print(f"Release {RELEASE_VERSION}...") item_ids = run_wiql(WIQL_QUERY) if not item_ids: print("No items matched the query.") return print(f"Found {len(item_ids)} item(s). Fetching details...") blocks = [] for item_id in item_ids: item = get_work_item(item_id) comments = get_comments(item_id) blocks.append(format_item(item, comments)) print(f" ✓ #{item_id}") # Compose the txt document header = "
".join([ f"TFS RELEASE NOTES DRAFT", f"Release version : {RELEASE_VERSION}", f"Generated : {datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')}", f"Total items : {len(blocks)}", "", ]) output = header + "
" + "

Done. File saved to: {OUTPUT_PATH}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() #!/usr/bin/env bash # TFS Release Notes Extractor # Scope: Features, User Stories, Bug Fixes. # Filters: "Include in Release Notes" checkbox and a release version. set -euo pipefail # exit on error, treat unset vars as errors, propagate pipe failures # Parameters TFS_BASE_URL="https://YOUR_TFS_SERVER/tfs/YOUR_COLLECTION/YOUR_PROJECT" # replace with TFS path RELEASE_VERSION="11.3" # replace with release version OUTPUT_PATH="$HOME/Desktop/dz_release_notes.txt" # Personal Access Token (get from User Settings > Security) PAT="YOUR_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN" # stub: replace with your PAT # Base64-encode the PAT for Basic Auth AUTH_HEADER="Authorization: Basic $(echo -n ":${PAT}" | base64)" # Helpers # Send authenticated GET request to TFS REST API tfs_get() { local endpoint="$1" curl --silent --fail \ --header "$AUTH_HEADER" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ "${TFS_BASE_URL}/_apis/${endpoint}" } # Send authenticated POST request tfs_post() { local endpoint="$1" local body="$2" curl --silent --fail \ --request POST \ --header "$AUTH_HEADER" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data "$body" \ "${TFS_BASE_URL}/_apis/${endpoint}" } # Strip HTML tags from Description and Release Notes strip_html() { echo "$1" | sed 's/<[^>]*>/ /g' | sed 's/ */ /g' | xargs } # TFS Query, WIQL echo "Querying TFS for release ${RELEASE_VERSION}..." WIQL_BODY=$(cat <<EOF { "query": "SELECT [System.Id], [System.Title], [System.WorkItemType] FROM WorkItems WHERE [System.WorkItemType] IN ('Feature', 'User Story', 'Bug') AND [Custom.IncludeInReleaseNotes] = True AND [Custom.ReleaseVersion] = '${RELEASE_VERSION}' ORDER BY [System.WorkItemType], [System.Id]" } EOF ) # Run the WIQL query and extract all work item IDs ITEM_IDS=$( tfs_post "wit/wiql?api-version=5.0" "$WIQL_BODY" \ | grep -o '"id":[0-9]*' \ # pull every "id":12345 occurrence | grep -o '[0-9]*' # strip the key, keep only the number ) if [[ -z "$ITEM_IDS" ]]; then echo "No items matched the query. Check your field names and filters." exit 0 fi ITEM_COUNT=$(echo "$ITEM_IDS" | wc -w | xargs) echo "Found ${ITEM_COUNT} item(s). Fetching details..." # Output txt file cat > "$OUTPUT_PATH" <<EOF TFS RELEASE NOTES RAW EXPORT Release version : ${RELEASE_VERSION} Generated : $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M') Total items : ${ITEM_COUNT} EOF # Script body for ITEM_ID in $ITEM_IDS; do # Fetch full work item details — $expand=all includes fields and relations ITEM_JSON=$(tfs_get "wit/workitems/${ITEM_ID}?\$expand=all&api-version=5.0") # Extract field values using grep + sed (no jq dependency required) ITEM_TYPE=$(echo "$ITEM_JSON" | grep -o '"System.WorkItemType":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/.*":"\(.*\)"/\1/') TITLE=$(echo "$ITEM_JSON" | grep -o '"System.Title":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/.*":"\(.*\)"/\1/') DESCRIPTION_RAW=$(echo "$ITEM_JSON" | grep -o '"System.Description":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/.*":"\(.*\)"/\1/') RELEASE_NOTES_RAW=$(echo "$ITEM_JSON" | grep -o '"Custom.ReleaseNotes":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/.*":"\(.*\)"/\1/') # NOTE: Custom.ReleaseNotes — replace with the actual reference name for # your Release Notes field if it differs. # Strip HTML from rich-text fields DESCRIPTION=$(strip_html "$DESCRIPTION_RAW") RELEASE_NOTES=$(strip_html "$RELEASE_NOTES_RAW") # Fetch comments for this item COMMENTS_JSON=$(tfs_get "wit/workitems/${ITEM_ID}/comments?api-version=5.0-preview" 2>/dev/null || echo "{}") COMMENTS=$(echo "$COMMENTS_JSON" | grep -o '"text":"[^"]*"' | sed 's/"text":"//;s/"$//' | nl -ba -nrz -w2) # Append the formatted block to the output file { echo "========================================================================" echo "[${ITEM_TYPE}] #${ITEM_ID} — ${TITLE}" echo "========================================================================" echo "" echo "DESCRIPTION" echo "----------------------------------------" echo "${DESCRIPTION:-"(empty)"}" echo "" echo "RELEASE NOTES" echo "----------------------------------------" echo "${RELEASE_NOTES:-"(empty)"}" echo "" echo "COMMENTS" echo "----------------------------------------" if [[ -n "$COMMENTS" ]]; then echo "$COMMENTS" else echo "(no comments)" fi echo "" } >> "$OUTPUT_PATH" echo " ✓ #${ITEM_ID}" done echo "" echo "Done. File saved to: ${OUTPUT_PATH}"

documents.t: Unlike the case studies in this portfolio, which describe real (anonymized) work, this artifact is an original demonstration built from scratch. DZ Data Hub is a fictional data platform — Snowflake as the warehouse, dbt for transformations, Airflow for orchestration, Metabase for consumption — and the simulator shows how I would document such a system so that every layer of it can be trusted, maintained, and explained. Open the simulator →

The simulator traces five billing events through a complete pipeline: a raw landing table, a dbt staging model, a conformed dimension, a fact table, and finally a governed business metric (Trial-to-Paid Conversion Rate). Press Run to watch one execution unfold stage by stage, or click any node in the DAG to read its documentation. The sample data is deliberately imperfect. The raw layer contains a duplicate event, an inconsistently cased event type, and an internal test account — the three most common data-quality problems in event pipelines. The documentation explains where each problem is handled, why it is handled there and nowhere else, and what contract each layer guarantees to the next.

Every node carries three layers of documentation, each written for a different reader: Overview — for consumers. Purpose, ownership, grain, schedule, and freshness guarantees in plain language, including explicit "do not query this table for reporting" guidance where it matters. Schema — the contract. Column-level descriptions that state not just what a field is, but what can be assumed about it (uniqueness, casing, timezone) and what cannot. Code — for maintainers. The commented source itself, where comments capture design intent rather than restating the syntax: why deduplication lives in staging and not in ingestion, why the fact table denormalizes account attributes, why a downstream filter would hide a regression instead of preventing one. The premise: documentation that lives in one narrative document goes stale, while documentation attached to the thing it describes — the model, the column, the DAG — stays honest. The simulator makes that structure tangible.

The final node treats a business metric as a documented, versioned object rather than a dashboard tile. Its page carries a canonical definition, split business/technical ownership, explicit caveats (the 30-day conversion window makes the latest month incomplete; account attributes reflect current state under SCD1), and a change log recording that the window was unified across dashboards in v1.2. Every convention shown in the metric — the acc_9xx test-account range, the naming, the window — is consistent with the upstream nodes, because that consistency is the whole point.

The simulator is a single self-contained React component: an SVG DAG with an animated execution run, a tabbed documentation panel, a stage-by-stage data preview, and a small hand-rolled syntax highlighter — no charting or diagram libraries. It respects prefers-reduced-motion and runs entirely in the browser. The IDE-style dark theme is intentional: the artifact is meant to read as a working tool, not a slide.

This portfolio collects writing samples from my most recent role at Hazeltree, a fintech SaaS platform for treasury management: cash optimization, portfolio profitability analysis, and financial risk management. The examples show how I turn complex product capabilities, workflows, and technical concepts into clear, concise, user-focused documentation — and the range of content I delivered as a Senior Technical Writer and writing team lead.

Examples of customer-facing documentation, including: Knowledge Base standard guides Getting Started With guides Conceptual overviews Step-by-step implementation instructions Each sample opens with a short summary that gives the context: intended audience, documentation objectives, and the business and compliance constraints it was written under.

The portfolio includes a Python automation script that I designed and built to streamline release note creation. The script pulls release information from TFS queries and consolidates it into a single structured file, removing hours of manual collection from every release cycle.

The portfolio also contains a release notes sample that shows my approach to release communication and delivery. It illustrates how I structure release information to improve readability, highlight customer impact, surface the changes that matter, and give stakeholders something they can act on.
